newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian election rivals agree to debate rematch.
newsitem.headline: Canadian election rivals agree to debate rematch.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien appeared to have reluctantly agreed on Thursday to a new election campaign debate on Quebec separation after an earlier one was aborted when its moderator collapsed.

Political and television company officials said the leaders of the five political parties had agreed in principle to a shorter French-language debate on the question of Quebec separation and would try to set the details later on Thursday.
"There is a tentative agreement to hold it," Reform Party spokesman Jim Armour told Reuters.
Chretien's rivals had suggested the Liberal leader, often not a stellar performer in impromptu situations, was chicken.
"Put your money where your mouth is. If you're actually ready to go there and make your case to Canadians that you have better ideas, come out from hiding," Conservative leader Jean Charest said.
"You're the only leader who's not ready to finish this debate on the unity of the country."

Chretien was grilled mercilessly in the debate in English on Monday. In the French debate the following night, he was just about to answer a question on Quebec when moderator Claire Lamarche passed out and fell off her chair.
The live television event was called off.

"People in Quebec don't want us to debate that anymore. They want us to be preoccupied with the real problems, you know, jobs and medicare and investment and social programs," Chretien said on Wednesday.

That prompted ridicule from Charest on the idea that the possibility of Canada falling apart was not a real problem. Quebec separatists came within a percentage point of winning a referendum on sovereignty in October 1995.

"I think the PM (prime minister) got mauled in the two debates, particularly the English one, when it got on to that, and I think they want to avoid the discussion," Reform Party leader Preston Manning said before the tentative agreement.
Chretien went into the debates with a lead of at least 20 points in the polls but the Liberal strategy has been to limit his exposure to unscripted situations.
He has, for example, held only one nationally televised news conference since calling the June 2 election on April 27, in stark contrast to most of his rivals.
Television officials helping to organize the debates said a conference call on Thursday afternoon would work on a venue, a date and the length of the rematch.
